first-principles-vs-analogy.core: Copy proven solutions when your context matches and stakes are low (analogy). Derive from bedrock facts when the problem is new, the stakes are high or your context differs (first principles). Know which mode you're in.

first_principles.problem: Engineers make architecture decisions that outlive the tools behind them. Most decisions are made by copying famous companies, which works until their hidden context doesn't match yours, and then you inherit their costs without their benefits.
truths: Tools change; constraints like physics, maths, budget and team size don't lie.
Copying is fast but assumes matching context.
derivation: Name the two modes: **analogy** (copy) and **first principles** (derive).
Watch for **cargo cults**: copying form without function.
Use the **algorithm**: assumptions → truths → rebuild → validate.
Pick the mode by **stakes, novelty and reversibility**.

analogy.title: The cook and the chef
analogy.story: The cook follows recipes and is efficient on routine nights. The chef understands what each ingredient does and can invent a dish when the pantry, altitude or guests change. A good kitchen needs both modes at the right time.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens have stable chemistry. Engineering constraints evolve with scale, so a first-principles answer must be re-derived as facts change.

example.title: Microservices for a 4-person startup
example.scenario: The CTO proposes microservices because Netflix uses them.

steps.label: Analogy check
steps.detail: Netflix has thousands of engineers needing independent deploys; this team has four.

steps.label: Truths
steps.detail: Each service adds deploys, monitoring and on-call that 4 people must run.

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: A well-structured monolith now, with clear module boundaries to split later.

example.outcome: the architecture fits today's facts, and the reasoning is written down so it can be revisited.

points: Copy form only if you also copy function.
Use the four-step algorithm for high-stakes calls.

check.q: When is reasoning by analogy the right choice?
check.a: For common, low-stakes, reversible decisions where your context matches the reference case.
Copying the visible form of a practice without the mechanism that made it work.

pattern-matching-vs-causal-reasoning.core: Pattern matching ("this looks like last time") is fast but follows correlation. Causal reasoning traces the mechanism that produced the symptom. Use fast instincts to mitigate and slow reasoning to find and design out root causes.

first_principles.problem: Incidents reward whoever speaks first, and the first explanation is usually a pattern match: the last deploy, last week's bug, two graphs moving together. Acting on correlation wastes time and leaves real causes in place.
truths: Correlation is everywhere in large metric sets.
Causes act through mechanisms you can describe and test.
Systems, not individuals, decide whether mistakes become outages.
derivation: Run **evidence-based Five Whys** ending in system fixes.
Use the causal chain to **design out failures** (timeouts, bulkheads, breakers).

analogy.title: A doctor diagnosing
analogy.story: A good doctor notices patterns ("flu season") but orders tests before prescribing, and then advises how to avoid the illness next time.
analogy.breaks: Patients describe symptoms. Systems only show metrics, so instrumentation decides how well you can reason.

example.title: An afternoon outage
example.scenario: DB CPU spikes right after a frontend deploy.

steps.label: Mitigate
steps.detail: Pause the backup job: the symptom clears.

steps.label: Cause
steps.detail: The table outgrew what the 3:00 backup could handle.

steps.label: Prevent
steps.detail: Add a scheduled-jobs view to the incident dashboard.

example.outcome: the real cause is fixed and the next responder sees scheduled jobs immediately.

check.q: What's the difference between correlation and causation?
check.a: Correlation means two things move together. Causation means one produces the other through a mechanism you can describe and test.

reversible-vs-irreversible-decisions.core: Classify decisions by the cost of reversing them. Move fast on two-way doors (Type 2), slow down on one-way doors (Type 1), and engineer escape hatches to turn the second into the first.

first_principles.problem: Organisations either debate everything (paralysis) or rush everything (lock-in). Both come from treating all decisions alike.
truths: Most decisions are cheap to reverse.
A few shape the system for years.
derivation: Assess on a **spectrum**: mechanism, time, impact, compounding.
**Convert** Type 1 to Type 2 with flags, abstractions, increments, pilots.
Set **approval thresholds** proportional to reversal cost.

analogy.title: Doors in a house
analogy.story: Most doors swing both ways and you walk through without thinking. A few lock behind you, and those you check carefully. And sometimes you can install a handle on the other side.
analogy.breaks: Doors are visibly different. Decision reversibility has to be assessed, and it changes over time.

example.title: A quarter of decisions
example.scenario: A platform team reviews how it made 40 decisions.

steps.label: Audit
steps.detail: Most delays came from cheap, reversible choices.

check.q: Which type of decision deserves an RFC?
check.a: Type 1 decisions with high impact and expensive reversal.

check.q: How can you make a Type 1 decision more reversible?
check.a: Feature flags, abstraction layers, incremental migration or pilots.

adrs-and-rfcs.core: Write down why, not just what. RFCs gather input before a significant decision; ADRs record each decision's context and consequences immutably, next to the code, so future engineers understand and can safely change it.

first_principles.problem: Organisations forget why systems are built the way they are. New engineers either fear changing anything or repeat old mistakes, and big decisions get made without input from the teams they affect.
derivation: Use **RFCs** before big, shared, irreversible decisions.
Record every significant decision in a short, immutable **ADR**.
Make it stick with **PR gates** and **tooling**.

analogy.title: Planning permission and the deeds
analogy.story: You apply for planning permission (RFC) before building, gathering comments. Once built, the deeds and notes (ADRs) record what was decided and why, for every future owner.
analogy.breaks: Property records are legally required. Decision records survive only if the team makes them part of the workflow.

example.title: A database migration end to end
example.scenario: The order service's database keeps failing.

steps.label: Years later
steps.detail: A new engineer reads 0007 before proposing a change.

example.outcome: decisions get better input up front and stay understandable for years.

check.q: What three sections form the core of an ADR?

the-iron-triangle.core: Velocity, reliability and cost compete for the same finite resources. Pick the two your business phase needs, measure all three, sacrifice the third on purpose, and use error budgets as the release valve.

first_principles.problem: Organisations want everything at once and end up sacrificing reliability silently, until outages and burnout force a reckoning.
derivation: Define each vertex with **metrics** (DORA, SLOs, full cost).
Choose by **business phase** and write it down.
Spot the triangle in **daily platform choices**.

analogy.title: Fast, good, cheap
analogy.story: The old contractor's sign: pick any two. Good contractors tell you which two you're getting before they start.
analogy.breaks: A contractor's job ends; a system keeps running, so the sacrificed side keeps costing.

example.title: A scale-up's yearly plan
example.scenario: Leadership plans next year's engineering priorities.

steps.label: Explicit
steps.detail: Cost will rise 30% for multi-AZ and SRE hires.

steps.label: Guard
steps.detail: An error budget policy decides freezes.

example.outcome: everyone knows what's being traded and why.

check.q: What does the Iron Triangle say you can't do?
check.a: Maximise velocity, reliability and cost efficiency simultaneously.

tradeoff-analysis.core: Every engineering choice gains something and gives something up. Name the axes, weigh options against your real constraints (including reversibility), choose deliberately, and record the reasoning.

first_principles.problem: Teams look for 'the right answer', copy popular choices, or decide by gut, then can't explain or revisit the decision later.
truths: True trade-offs worsen one quality to improve another.
Context decides which downsides are tolerable.
Reversibility changes how careful you must be.
derivation: Name recurring **axes**: simplicity/flexibility, build/buy, lock-in, speed/safety.
Use the **five-step framework** and record an ADR.

analogy.title: Buying the right car for your life
analogy.story: There's no best car. A family of five and a city commuter choose differently, and both are right.
analogy.breaks: Cars are easy to compare on paper. Software costs often appear later, so seek real experience reports.

example.title: Picking an auth solution

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.detail: Build fails on TCO and security risk.

example.outcome: a clear, recorded choice that can be challenged with data later.

check.q: What makes something a true trade-off?
check.a: Improving one quality necessarily degrades another.

risk-modeling.core: Risk = likelihood × impact. Write risks down, score them consistently, put a price on them, choose a deliberate response, find silent failures with FMEA, and build general resilience for what you can't predict.

first_principles.problem: Engineering decisions are bets, but most teams never name them. Risks live in people's heads, priorities follow fear rather than exposure, and silent failures surprise everyone.
derivation: Use **FMEA** for detection gaps; build **resilience** for black swans.

analogy.title: Running a household
analogy.story: You insure the house, fix the leaking roof first, list what needs maintenance, and keep an emergency fund for what you can't foresee.
analogy.breaks: Households have decades of shared wisdom. Systems need their own analysis.

example.title: A platform team's first risk review

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Untested backups and silent cron failures move to the top.

example.outcome: risk becomes a managed portfolio instead of a source of surprises.

check.q: What are the four risk responses?

strangler-fig-migration.core: Don't rewrite legacy systems in one big bang. Put a proxy in front, replace one slice at a time, sync data carefully (shared DB, dual writes, CDC), shift traffic gradually, and actually delete the old code.

first_principles.problem: Legacy monoliths are scary to change and tempting to rewrite. Big-bang rewrites freeze the business, chase a moving target and miss hidden rules.
truths: Data is shared and hard to split.

analogy.title: The strangler fig
analogy.story: A fig grows around a host tree, slowly taking over until the host is gone and the fig stands alone.
analogy.breaks: Figs need no budget. Migrations need sustained funding and clear completion goals.

example.title: Migrating a billing monolith

steps.label: Progress
steps.detail: Tracked by % of endpoints migrated each quarter.

example.outcome: the legacy system is replaced without a single big-risk cutover.
